_comment: Copy this to the audited repo and delete the underscore keys. Preferred location
is .tld/quality-sweep-baseline.json; if the repo gitignores .tld/, use
.claude/quality-sweep-baseline.json or quality-sweep-baseline.json at the root, so
the file is committed and reviewed like any other code. An uncommitted baseline
forgets everything between runs, which defeats the entire point of the check.
Nothing in this file may be time-bound. No month, no year, no 'as of' notes, no
expected finding counts that a landed fix would invalidate. It is read unattended
for years, and a stale constant does not raise an error, it just quietly stops
matching. Dates appear in exactly one place: last_completed, which is written from
the real clock and only ever compared as a delta, never to a literal.
The one exception to project-neutrality: this file is where every project-specific
thing goes. The engine and the skill next to it name no project on purpose.

_comment_labels: family_label is the STABLE label every filed ticket carries and the de-dup search
looks for. The lens label is derived from it as <family_label>-<lens>.
NO LABEL CARRIES A DATE. Not a year, not a month, not a week, in any position or
format, here or in ticket_labels or in a lens's topic_labels. A sweep runs weekly,
so a month in a label is stamped by four or five different runs and identifies none
of them, and a day in a label is a fresh unsearchable string every week: coarse and
it cannot name the run, fine and it cannot be searched for. The date goes in the
ticket's provenance block and in the run document's filename, which is exactly what
makes a past run findable months later. Documents are dated; labels are not.
_comment_tracker: Only needed when the repo has no .tld/campaign.md. That file always wins.
Leave these empty and the skill reports findings in full, says no tracker is
configured, and names the keys that would enable filing. It never guesses.
_comment_vocabulary: The next three maps are this project's whole label vocabulary. Declaring them is
what lets a backlog check tell policy from rot: a label on a ticket that is not a
sweep label and appears in none of these maps is UNDECLARED, and the right move is
to report it and say which ticket carries it, never to guess which it is and act.
All three are OPTIONAL and start empty. A project with no taxonomy of its own
leaves them empty and only the sweep labels above are ever applied. Filling one in
is a decision somebody made, so each entry carries its reason as the value.
The governing rule is ONE FACT, ONE HOME: never carry in a label what a field on
the ticket already holds. A label and a field meaning the same thing drift apart
silently, because the ticket keeps looking correct in whichever one you read.
_comment_forbidden_labels: Label families this project deleted, and the reason each one went. Report any open
ticket carrying one; never recreate them. Most entries here will be labels that
duplicated a field: a 'bug' label beside an issue-type field, a priority label
beside a priority field, a whose-queue label beside a status field.
_comment_area_labels: What part of the product a ticket touches, one label per area. This is the one
legitimate exception to 'one fact, one home', and only where the tracker has no
field that holds it: Jira components are the native home, and a project with no
components defined, and no tooling able to create one, has nowhere else to put it.
An exception, not a precedent. Fixed vocabulary: pick from the list, never invent
one mid-run, and raise the gap if nothing fits. An area nobody filters by is noise.
_comment_theme_labels: Named work clusters. An area label says what part of the product a ticket touches;
a theme label says which push it belongs to, which is a different question and
often spans areas. Optional per ticket. Includes quality dimensions that cut across
areas, such as accessibility or security, which a human filing by hand has no other
way to name. The sweeps themselves must not apply these: a sweep's ticket is already
labelled with the lens that found it.
_comment_sibling_labels: The stable labels of the OTHER recurring checks that read this same repository and
file into this same tracker. Step 4b searches these in addition to the family label.
Without them the de-dup is blind to a sibling audit ticket and files a duplicate of it.
Leave the list empty if this is the only recurring check the project runs.
Never dated, for the same reason no other label is dated.
_comment_max_run: Wall-clock envelope in minutes. The engine prints a DEADLINE from it and forces
PARTIAL once it passes, so a long sweep cannot spill into a working day and cannot
report clean after overrunning. Stopping early is allowed; stopping early and
_comment_non_signals: Tool output that is loud and meaningless in this project. A finding resting on one
of these is not a finding. Every project has at least one, and writing it down is
what stops the same non-finding being re-investigated every single week.
non_signals: the type checker's error count on this repo, which is dominated by one known config issue
the root linter's exit code, which is non-zero on a clean tree and is not gated in CI
_comment_do_not_raise: Topics a human has already settled and does not want re-litigated. Re-raising one
wastes a whole run's attention. Each needs the reason, so a later reader can tell a
settled decision from a forgotten one.

do_not_raise.topic: example: adding a default value to the location picker
do_not_raise.reason: deliberate product decision, the prompt is the feature

_comment_lenses: One entry per standing question. rank drives which gets a scheduled slot first, so
the most impactful runs while there is budget left. Run lenses in straight rank
order: alternating them looks fairer and is worse, because whichever slot runs dry
then loses the same top-ranked lens every week.
focus_areas is the sweep's precision and the only field that can make it lie in both
directions. An area you forget to declare is never looked at; an area declared too
broadly spends the budget everywhere and finds nothing anywhere.
topic_labels is EMPTY here on purpose, and most projects should leave it empty. The
engine prints it to the run as part of 'LABELS for anything filed', so whatever sits
here is what the run puts on a ticket regardless of what the task wrapper says. That
is worth knowing before you fill it in: a wrapper corrected without correcting this
file changes nothing, and a name listed here that the project also forbids makes the
baseline order a label the same baseline reports as a violation. The lens is already
named by the <family_label>-<lens> label, and the run by the ticket's provenance block.
preflight lists what must be reachable before the sweep starts. A failed preflight is
a SKIPPED RUN, never a clean pass, and never a reason to substitute a shallower check.
last_completed is written from the real clock, and only when a run finished COMPLETE.
A lens being starved of budget week after week shows up as a growing number here
rather than as silence, which is the only way that failure is ever visible.

bug-hunt.title: Bug hunt
focus_areas: writes that can half-complete and still report success
arithmetic on quantities or money that mixes units or currencies
visibility and permission checks that differ between the client and the server
state that two code paths can update concurrently
bug-hunt.severity_scale: S1 data loss or wrong output a user acts on, S2 wrong behaviour with a workaround, S3 narrow or cosmetic
bug-hunt.evidence_bar: name the input, the code path, and the wrong output. A finding that cannot name all three is unconfirmed, reported and filed as such, never dropped
bug-hunt.granularity: one ticket per root cause, naming every affected site

benign_patterns.pattern: a client-side check with no server equivalent in the same file
benign_patterns.why: the server enforces it in its own layer. Confirm by reading the enforcing code, never by reading a comment claiming it exists

performance.title: Performance
focus_areas: queries that fetch every row to compute a small aggregate
requests issued once per item in a list
bundle weight and what is loaded before first paint
refetch loops caused by an unstable dependency
performance.severity_scale: S1 grows without bound with data size, S2 fixed but large, S3 measurable but small
performance.evidence_bar: name the payload, the count, or the byte size. A finding with no number is unconfirmed
performance.granularity: one ticket per pattern, naming every call site
preflight: the package manager can install dependencies offline or the tree is already installed

benign_patterns.pattern: a list query with no pagination on a table that is bounded by design
benign_patterns.why: the row count has a hard ceiling set elsewhere. Confirm the ceiling exists in code, not in an assumption

_comment_benign: Cross-lens benign patterns. The finders are told to over-flag on purpose, because a
check tuned until it is quiet is a check that has stopped working. This list is what
makes that affordable: triage becomes a lookup rather than a fresh investigation.
Every entry needs the reason, written for someone who was not there.
Set lens to a slug to scope an entry, or omit it to apply everywhere.

benign_patterns.pattern: generated files under a build output directory
benign_patterns.why: not written by hand and replaced on every build, so a finding there is a finding about the generator

_comment_accepted: Reviewed exceptions. Adding an object here is a SIGN-OFF: it means somebody opened
the file, read the code, and concluded the sweep is over-flagging on something
genuinely fine. It is never a way to make a noisy check quiet, and a reason that only
says 'known' or 'by design' is not a reason.
object is <lens>::<repo-relative path>::<symbol>, matched exactly. Renaming the file
or the symbol detaches the row, so re-point it in the same edit as the rename.

accepted.reason: the query looks unbounded but the table is capped at one row per lab by a unique constraint, verified in the schema

_comment_known_open: Findings already tracked by an open ticket. The next run reports these as KNOWN-OPEN
instead of re-triaging them, and never re-files them.
PRUNE A ROW WHEN ITS TICKET CLOSES. A closed key left here suppresses the finding
forever, which is the one way this check goes quiet while the defect is still in the
tree. Step 3 re-checks the status of every key precisely because this gets forgotten.
Findings that are re-detected after their ticket CLOSED are filed as a regression of
that key, which is the most valuable thing a recurring check produces. That is why
closed tickets are deliberately never seeded into this list.
